Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Say the care line first: anyone can step out. Some students have lost someone. Name the Good Samaritan law clearly, and check in quietly with anyone who seemed shaken.

Every student in the room

Some students have lost a family member or friend to an overdose, and some fear calling 911; name the Good Samaritan law clearly and let anyone step out who needs to.

Slide 4 · Notes

Fentanyl isn’t mixed evenly when pills are pressed. Two pills from the same batch can hold completely different amounts. Half a pill can hold all of it.

Slide 5 · Notes

A few guesses out loud. Then: a coin flip is not a safety plan.

Slide 6 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 7 · Notes

Opioids, including fentanyl, oxycodone and heroin, hit receptors in the reward circuit and in a small brainstem cluster that sets the rhythm of every breath. Enough of them and the rhythm stalls. Ask: why might someone overdosing look like they’re just asleep? (Snoring or gurgling, no response.)

Slide 8 · Notes

Thumbs up or down, then the answer. Say it slowly: fewer teens using, more teens dying, because the supply changed.

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 13 · Notes

Take a few. Then: today fixes the last one.

Slide 14 · Notes

Walk each step, then the pair drill. To check: shout their name and rub the breastbone hard. Expect the person to wake up sick, shaky or angry; that’s withdrawal.

Slide 15 · Notes

Narcan is sold over the counter. Ask: where is it kept at school?

Slide 16 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 17 · Notes

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why a pill that didn't come from a pharmacy can contain fentanyl, how an opioid overdose stops breathing, and the five steps to take if it happens in front of them: Recognize, Call, Narcan, Breathe, Stay. The focus is helping a friend. Nobody's own use comes up.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards for the exit card
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 4 minReal or fake? Move to a wall
  2. 5 minThe cookie, and the DEA guess
  3. 5 minHow an overdose stops breathing
  4. 5 minThe data: deaths rose, and who was nearby
  5. 4 minWhy people freeze: turn and talk, share out
  6. 10 minThe five steps and the pair drill
  7. 3 minThe Narcan myth, and the Good Samaritan law
  8. 5 minThree moments: Hannah, Luke, after the Narcan
  9. 4 minWrite the text, every student, exit card

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Real or fake, the cookie, the bystander guess, the five steps with the pair drill, and the exit card.

Before you teach
Some students have lost someone.

Overdose has touched many families. Say at the start that this topic is close for some people and anyone can step out or pass. Afterward, check in quietly with anyone who looked shaken and walk them to a counselor if they want.

Keep it about helping a friend.

Never ask about anyone's own use. Frame every question as "if you saw this" or "people our age." That framing keeps the room open.

Show the naloxone if you can.

Holding the box makes the steps real. The nasal spray has been sold over the counter since 2023, and it can't hurt someone who isn't on opioids.

Be exact about the Good Samaritan law.

In Massachusetts, neither the caller nor the person overdosing can be charged with drug possession for calling. It covers possession, not every possible charge. Say both halves.

If a student says they've bought pills.

Thank them, stay calm, and walk them to a counselor or the nurse that day. A pill that didn't come from a pharmacy is the danger, and they just told you something that matters.

Expect the "fake pill" fear to spread to real meds.

Some students take prescribed medication. Be clear: a pill from a pharmacy with your name on the label is the safe kind.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Grief in the room.

Overdose deaths reach every kind of family and neighborhood. Avoid any picture of who "those people" are. The person who died may be someone's parent, sibling or cousin.

Fear of police.

For some students, calling 911 raises worries about immigration status or how police treat their community. Name it, explain the Good Samaritan law, and be clear that a stopped-breathing emergency is still a 911 call.

Family members in recovery.

Some students have a parent in recovery, on medication like methadone or buprenorphine, or still using. Talk about overdose as a medical emergency and addiction as a health problem, never as a character flaw.

Pharmacy access.

"Get it from a pharmacy" assumes insurance and a doctor. Mention that naloxone is sold over the counter and that the nurse or a counselor can help find free sources.

Faith and culture.

Some families don't talk about drugs at all. Students may be the first in their house to learn this. The take-home link lets them share it at home if they want.

Neurodivergent students.

Students with ADHD may hear about "Adderall" from a plug. Note that fake study pills have contained fentanyl and meth, and that a real prescription comes with a doctor who can adjust it.

What the research says

22 U.S. teens aged 14 to 18 died of a drug overdose each week in 2022, while teen drug use was falling. Most deaths involved fentanyl, often in counterfeit pills.

Friedman and Hadland, New England Journal of Medicine, 2024

Of U.S. overdose deaths among 10 to 19 year olds from mid-2019 to 2021, 84% involved illicit fentanyl and about 1 in 4 had evidence of counterfeit pills. Two out of three had a potential bystander nearby.

Tanz et al., CDC MMWR, 2022

Opioid receptors in two small brainstem sites account for the slowed breathing that kills in an overdose.

Bachmutsky et al., eLife, 2020 (mouse study)

Half of the fake pills the DEA tested in 2024 contained a potentially deadly dose of fentanyl (2 milligrams), down from 7 in 10 in 2023.

U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, 2024

Narcan nasal spray was approved for over-the-counter sale in 2023.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2023

Xylazine, an animal sedative often mixed with fentanyl, isn't reversed by naloxone, but naloxone still reverses the fentanyl mixed with it.

CDC, Xylazine: What clinicians need to know

In Massachusetts, a person who calls for help in an overdose, and the person overdosing, can't be charged with drug possession because of the call.

Massachusetts General Laws, chapter 94C, section 34A
